profile.name: Melinting dance
profile.tagline: A 16th-century royal dance from Lampung, Indonesia, symbolizing gratitude and majesty.
profile.insight: In 1965, President Sukarno renamed the 16th-century 'Cetik Kipas' dance to 'Melinting,' marking its transition from a private royal ritual of the Lampung nobility to a national stage performance.
profile.profile: The Melinting dance is a traditional performance from the Lampung province of Indonesia, originating in the 16th century under the reign of Ratu Melinting II. Originally a restricted royal ritual, the dance serves to express gratitude and demonstrate the majesty of the Melinting kingdom. Today, it is performed by eight dancers—four men and four women—who navigate through specific rounds including the opening, the kugowo queen, the floating kenui, and the closing. The dance is characterized by its distinct costume, which incorporates Islamic influences alongside traditional Lampung elements like tapis cloth and gold headgear.
profile.profile_long:
The Melinting dance serves as a historical relic of the Melinting Kingdom in Lampung, Indonesia. Created in the 16th century by Ratu Melinting II, the dance was initially a private ritual exclusive to the royal family. Its primary purpose was to express gratitude for happiness and to demonstrate the power and majesty of the kingdom. The dance remained a restricted royal practice until 1958, when it underwent a refinement process that eventually allowed for its broader performance. In 1965, at the request of President Sukarno, the dance was performed at Istora Senayan in Jakarta, where it was officially transitioned from its original name, 'Cetik Kipas,' to 'Melinting.'

The performance structure requires eight dancers, balanced equally between four men and four women. The choreography is organized into distinct rounds: the opening (Pembuka), the kugowo queen round, the floating kenui round, and the closing (Penutup). The movements are categorized by gender, though specific technical footwork and postural requirements are not described in sources. The dance is accompanied by traditional Lampung musical instruments, including the Kalo Bala, kendang, gongs, gamelan, and fiddle, which serve to signal the opening of the dance, accompany the dancers' entrance, and show respect to guests.

Costuming reflects a blend of traditional Lampung culture and Islamic influence. Men wear tapis cloth, a belanga shirt, seretei feathers, a gold skullcap, and carry a fan. Women wear tapis pepadun, a long-sleeved white kebaya, a bun, a yellow veil, jukum fruit, and a ruwi bracelet, also carrying a fan. Make-up is considered a critical component of the performance to establish the appropriate atmosphere. Despite its historical significance, the dance remains relatively obscure even within the Lampung region itself.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the 16th century under Ratu Melinting II in Lampung. It was historically a private royal ritual until it was refined in 1958 and renamed from 'Cetik Kipas' to 'Melinting' by President Sukarno in 1965.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves eight performers, four men and four women. The performance is divided into four rounds: opening, kugowo queen, floating kenui, and closing. Specific footwork, posture, and counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music utilizes traditional Lampung instruments including Kalo Bala, kendang, gongs, gamelan, and fiddle. The music serves to accompany the entrance of dancers and signal respect for guests.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear tapis cloth, belanga shirts, seretei feathers, gold skullcaps, and fans. Women wear tapis pepadun, white kebaya, yellow veils, jukum fruit, ruwi bracelets, and fans. Make-up is essential to the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed at traditional events to welcome guests. It symbolizes gratitude for happiness and the majesty of the Melinting kingdom.
sections.notable_figures: Ratu Melinting II (creator) and President Sukarno (who renamed the dance).
sections.lineage: The dance is a relic of the Melinting Kingdom and is associated with the development of Islam in the region.

profile.sacred_note: Historically a private royal ritual of the Queen Melinting family, now performed for guests and public events.

claims.text: The Melinting dance is a traditional dance from Lampung province, Indonesia, which existed in the sixteenth century.
claims.quote: Melinting is one of the traditional dances from Lampung province, Indonesia. It was originally known as the Cetik Kipas dance before its name was changed to Melinting dance. ... Melinting is a dance inherited from Ratu Melinting, which is estimated to have existed in the sixteenth century.

claims.text: The dance was renamed Melinting at the request of President Sukarno in 1965.
claims.quote: The name change was proposed by President Sukarno, who asked the Central Lampung Regional Government to perform the dance at Istora Senayan Jakarta on August 17, 1965.

claims.text: The dance was created by Ratu Melinting II and served to show gratitude and the majesty of the kingdom.
claims.quote: This dance is one of the relics of the Melinting Kingdom, which was created by Ratu Melinting II in the 16th century. This dance has the meaning of showing how people are grateful for the happiness they have received. In addition, this dance also illustrates the might and majesty of Ratu Meliting in leading the kingdom at that time.

claims.text: The dance is performed by eight dancers, four men and four women, divided into four rounds.
claims.quote: The movements in dancing are divided into two categories based on gender, with a total of eight dancers: four men and four women. When dancing, the dancers will be divided into several rounds, the opening round (Pembuka), the kugowo queen round, the floating kenui round, and the closing round (Penutup).

claims.text: The dance uses various musical instruments including Kalo Bala, kendang, gongs, gamelan, and fiddle.
claims.quote: Melinting dance uses various musical accompaniments typical of the people of Lampung, one of which is Kalo Bala. Besides Kalo Bala, the accompaniment of this dance also often uses kendang, gongs, gamelan, fiddle, and various other musical instruments.

claims.text: Before 1958, the dance was exclusively owned by the royal family.
claims.quote: Before undergoing a refinement change in 1958, the Melinting Lampung dance was absolutely owned by the royal family of the Queen Melinting Family.
